title: Six Clever Machines
subtitle: Levers, pulleys, ramps and the tricks that make hard jobs easy
subject: Physics

p: Yes, you. With the right tool, an 8-year-old can lift one side of a car off the ground. Garage workers do it every day with a jack, and a jack is just a screw or a lever wearing a disguise.

Machines do not give you free strength. They play a trick. They let you push with a small force over a long distance instead of a big force over a short one. Six simple machines do almost all of this trickery. Let's meet them.
pages.cap: A long lever lets a small push lift a heavy load.
pages.fact: Did you know? Scientists in ancient Greece listed five simple machines about 2,000 years ago, and the ramp was added around the year 1600. People used all six thousands of years before that.

p: Here is the rule behind every simple machine. Moving a load takes a certain amount of work. Work is force times distance. You cannot make the work smaller. But you can swap the two parts.

Lift a 20 kg box straight up 1 m, and you need a 20 kg push. Slide it up a gentle ramp 4 m long, and you only need about a 5 kg push. You pushed four times as far, with a quarter of the force. The work is the same. It just felt easier.
pages.cap: A longer path means a lighter push.
pages.fact: Did you know? Scientists measure force in newtons. One apple pulls down on your hand with about 1 newton.

p: A lever is a stiff bar that tips on a point called the fulcrum. A seesaw is a lever. So is a crowbar, a hammer pulling a nail, and a spoon flicking peas.

Sit far from the middle of a seesaw and you can balance someone much heavier who sits close to it. A 25 kg child sitting 2 m from the fulcrum balances a 50 kg adult sitting 1 m from it. Distance makes up for weight. The longer your side of the lever, the bigger the load you can lift.
pages.cap: A seesaw: a small weight far out balances a big weight close in.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Greek thinker Archimedes said that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could move the whole Earth.

p: Levers come in three flavours, depending on where the fulcrum sits.

In a seesaw or scissors, the fulcrum is in the middle. In a wheelbarrow or a nutcracker, the load is in the middle and the fulcrum is at the end. In a fishing rod, a broom or your own arm, the push is in the middle. Your elbow is the fulcrum, your muscle pulls near it, and your hand swings far and fast. That is why you can throw a ball much faster than your muscle actually moves.
pages.cap: A balance scale is a lever with the fulcrum exactly in the middle.

pages.q: On a seesaw, how can a light child balance a heavy adult?
pages.why: The farther you sit from the fulcrum, the more your weight counts. Distance makes up for weight.

p: Try dragging a loaded sled across a floor. Now put it on a wagon. Suddenly it rolls with a finger push. Wheels beat dragging because only a tiny patch of the wheel touches the ground at a time, so there is far less rubbing.

The oldest wheel ever found was dug up in Slovenia. It is about 5,150 years old. The axle is the rod through the middle. Turn a big wheel and the small axle turns with great force. A doorknob, a steering wheel and a screwdriver all work this way.
pages.cap: A cart on wheels: the first wheels carried loads, not people.
pages.fact: Did you know? The first wheels may have been potter's wheels for shaping clay, not cart wheels.

p: The Great Pyramid of Egypt was once 146 m tall, higher than a 40-storey building. It holds about 2.3 million stone blocks, most weighing more than 2 tonnes. Workers dragged them up long ramps of earth and brick, one block at a time.
A ramp, also called an inclined plane, is the simplest machine of all. It does not even move. A flat surface tilted up. That is it.

Wheelchair ramps, loading ramps on trucks, roads winding up a mountain and slides at the park are all ramps. The gentler the slope, the less force you need, but the farther you travel. A road that zigzags up a mountain is a ramp folded back and forth so cars never have to climb straight up.
pages.cap: A ball rolls down a ramp and keeps going; a load rolls up one with a gentle push.
pages.fact: Did you know? Canadian building rules say a wheelchair ramp should rise no more than 1 m for every 12 m of length.

p: Take two ramps and stick them back to back. Now you have a wedge. A wedge is a ramp that moves. Push it forward, and it pushes sideways, splitting things apart.

An axe is a wedge. So is a knife, a nail, a pin, a doorstop and the front of a ship cutting through water. Your front teeth are wedges too. Thin, sharp wedges split with less force, which is why a sharp knife is actually safer than a dull one: you do not have to push as hard.
pages.cap: A ship's pointed bow is a wedge that parts the water.
pages.fact: Did you know? A zipper is a set of three tiny wedges that push the teeth apart or squeeze them together.

pages.h: Try it: lift a heavy book with one finger
p: Build a lever and feel the trick for yourself.
steps: Put a 30 cm ruler on a table with a pencil or an eraser under it, near one end. The pencil is your fulcrum.
Rest a heavy book on the short end of the ruler.
Press down on the long end with one finger. The book lifts.
Now slide the pencil to the middle of the ruler and try again. Harder, right?
Move the pencil until you find the easiest spot.
pages.cap: The longer your side of the lever, the easier the lift.
pages.safe: Keep fingers clear of the gap under the book.

p: Wrap a ramp around a pole and you get a screw. The spiral ridge is called the thread. Each turn moves the screw forward only a tiny bit, but with a huge force. That is why a small screwdriver can pull a screw deep into hard wood.

Jar lids, bolts, light bulbs, piano stools and a spiral staircase are all screws. More than 2,000 years ago, Archimedes used a giant screw inside a tube to lift water uphill. Farmers in Egypt still use Archimedes screws today.
pages.cap: A screw thread is a long, gentle ramp curled into a spiral.
pages.fact: Did you know? A car jack with a screw can lift a 1,500 kg car with the strength of one arm.

pages.q: Which simple machine is a knife?
pages.why: A knife blade is two ramps back to back. Pushing it forward pushes the food apart sideways. That is a wedge.

p: A pulley is a wheel with a groove for a rope. Loop the rope over it and pull down, and the load goes up. One pulley does not make the load lighter. It changes the direction of your pull, so you can use your weight and pull down instead of lifting up.

Flagpoles, window blinds, clotheslines and cranes all use pulleys. Elevators hang from steel ropes running over pulleys at the top of the shaft, with a heavy counterweight on the other end to balance the car.
pages.cap: Pull down, and the load rises.
pages.fact: Did you know? Sailors were using pulleys more than 2,000 years ago to haul up heavy sails and cargo.

p: Here is where pulleys get clever. Thread the rope through two pulleys, one fixed above and one hanging on the load, and you only need half the force. Four pulleys, a quarter. The catch is the trade you already know: you have to pull twice or four times as much rope.

A set of pulleys working together is called a block and tackle. With six pulleys, one adult can lift a 500 kg piano. Construction cranes lift 10 tonne steel beams the same way, with a motor doing the pulling.
pages.cap: More pulleys, lighter pull, longer rope.
pages.fact: Did you know? The word tackle comes from an old Dutch word for the ropes and gear on a ship.

p: Gears are wheels with teeth. Mesh two together and turning one turns the other. They are really a wheel and axle with a grip, so we count them with the six, but they deserve their own page.

Gears can change speed. A gear with 40 teeth turning a gear with 10 teeth makes the small one spin four times for every single turn of the big one. Faster, but weaker. Turn it around, big gear driven by small, and you get slow and strong. Clocks, bikes, whisks and car engines are full of gears.
pages.cap: Three meshing gears: each one turns the opposite way from its neighbour.
pages.fact: Did you know? A mechanical watch can hold more than 100 tiny gears and springs inside a case the size of a coin.

pages.h: Shift gears, and the same legs climb any hill
p: A bike in a low gear turns the back wheel less than once for every turn of the pedals. Easy to push, slow to go. In a high gear, one pedal turn spins the wheel three or four times. Hard to push, fast to go.

pages.q: A big gear with 40 teeth turns a small gear with 10 teeth. When the big gear turns once, how many times does the small gear turn?
pages.why: Forty teeth pass by for one turn of the big gear. The small gear uses 10 teeth per turn, so it turns 4 times.

p: Every machine has a sneaky enemy. Friction is the rubbing between two surfaces that slide across each other. It turns some of your push into heat and wasted effort. Rub your hands together fast and feel it.

That is why real ramps need more push than the maths says, and why the oldest pulleys squeaked. People fight friction with oil, grease, wax, smooth metal and ball bearings, which are tiny steel balls that let a wheel roll instead of rub. A well-oiled bike loses only a few percent of your effort to friction.
pages.cap: Friction turns motion into heat, like a hot cup warming a thermometer.
pages.fact: Did you know? Space probes keep spinning for years because, with no air, there is almost nothing to rub against.

p: You do not have to build simple machines. You were born with them. Your arms and legs are levers that tip at your joints. Your jaw is a lever, and your teeth are wedges. The round bone of your kneecap works like a pulley, guiding the tendon over the joint so your leg can straighten with more force.
Even your skeleton of 206 bones is a frame of levers pulled by about 600 muscles. When you jump, your calf muscle pulls with a force more than twice your body weight.
pages.cap: A skeleton is a set of levers; muscles are the pullers.
pages.fact: Did you know? A grasshopper's leg is such a good lever that it can jump 20 times its own body length.

p: A medieval castle was a toolbox of simple machines. The drawbridge was a lever, lifted by chains running over pulleys. The portcullis, a heavy iron gate, slid up on ropes wound around a wheel and axle called a windlass.

Attackers brought their own machines. A trebuchet was a giant lever with a heavy box of stones on the short end. When the box dropped, the long arm whipped round and flung a 100 kg rock more than 200 m at the castle walls.
pages.cap: Drawbridge, gate and winch: the castle ran on levers and wheels.
pages.fact: Did you know? In the 1990s, a full-size trebuchet built in England threw a small car.

pages.h: Try it: measure the ramp trick
p: Use a rubber band as a force meter and see how much a ramp helps.
steps: Tie a rubber band to a toy car or a small box with a loop of string.
Lift the car straight up by the rubber band. Measure how much the band stretches with a ruler. Write it down.
Lean a board or a big book against a stack of books to make a ramp.
Pull the car slowly up the ramp by the band. Measure the stretch again.
Make the ramp longer and gentler. Measure once more. Which stretch is smallest?
pages.cap: Less stretch means less force. The gentler ramp wins.
pages.safe: Pull slowly so the rubber band does not snap back.

p: Join two or more simple machines and you get a compound machine. Scissors are two levers crossed at a fulcrum, with wedge-shaped blades. A wheelbarrow is a lever riding on a wheel and axle. A can opener has a lever, a wedge and a gear.

A bicycle might be the best compound machine ever built. Pedals are levers. Wheels are wheels and axles. Gears and a chain carry the push. Brakes are levers. Every bolt is a screw. Together they let you travel 4 times faster than walking with the same effort.
pages.cap: A bridge, like a bike, is many simple parts working as one machine.
pages.fact: Did you know? A modern car contains more than 30,000 parts, and most of them are simple machines.

pages.q: Which of these is a compound machine, made of more than one simple machine?
pages.why: Scissors combine two levers with two wedge-shaped blades. A ramp and a doorstop are each one simple machine.

p: The simple machines never went away. They just grew. A tower crane is a lever balanced on a mast, with pulleys on the arm and gears in the motor. The tallest cranes reach more than 200 m and lift 60 tonnes.

A mountain cable car is a pulley system with a loop of steel rope several kilometres long. A rollercoaster is a ramp with a chain lift, a wheel and axle that drags the cars to the top. Then gravity does the rest. Look at any big machine and you can find the six inside.
pages.cap: Wheels, levers and gears: a train is the six machines on rails.
pages.fact: Did you know? The Peak 2 Peak gondola in Whistler, British Columbia, hangs from cables 436 m above the valley floor.

p: From now on you will see simple machines hiding all around you. A door is a lever that tips on its hinges. A toilet handle is a lever. A tap is a screw. A rolling pin is a wheel and axle. A stapler is a lever and a wedge. The teeth of a zipper, the edge of a shovel, the slide at the park.
People built the pyramids, sailed oceans and raised cathedrals with nothing but these six ideas and strong backs. Now you know the tricks too.
pages.cap: Look closely: the six machines are in every room of your home.
pages.fact: Did you know? A pencil sharpener uses a wedge, a screw, and a wheel and axle all at once.

items: Force multiplied by the distance you move something.
A stiff bar that tips on a point to lift or move a load.
The point a lever tips on.
A wheel fixed to a rod through its centre, so turning one turns the other.
A ramp: a flat surface tilted up.
Two ramps back to back; it splits things apart when pushed.
A ramp wrapped in a spiral around a pole.
A grooved wheel that a rope runs over to lift a load.
A wheel with teeth that turns another toothed wheel.
The rubbing between surfaces that slows motion and makes heat.
A machine made of two or more simple machines.

qs: If you could only keep one of the six simple machines in the world, which would you choose, and what would we lose without the others?
Simple machines make work easier but never smaller. Is there anything in life like that?
Design a machine to lift your backpack onto a shelf using at least two simple machines. How would it work?
